title: developer-knobs-latency-econ-snapshot-may14-2027
content:
Purpose:
This is a short internal snapshot aimed at developer-facing collateral for the Console and API docs. It catalogues the most impactful runtime knobs (batch size, kv_cache, quantization level, prewarm policy, routing tier) and shows rough latency vs cost tradeoffs with simple ascii charts and recommended presets for common developer intents (interactive latency-sensitive vs throughput-first vs cost-min).

Audience/context:
- Product-Optimize + Developer Experience.
- Not a final benchmarking artifact — numbers are illustrative (small-sample bench on staging GPUs, mixed request shapes). Use for copy, console slider defaults, and quick help tips.

High-level takeaways (TL;DR):
- Biggest single win for steady interactive p50 is keeping kv_cache hit-rates > 70% (saves ~15–30% p95 depending on model length).
- Dynamic batching reduces per-token cost by 20–40% at throughput >300 RPS but increases p95 by 10–60ms for short-turn workloads.
- Quantization (int8/ggml-type) reduces cost 25–50% with a modest p50 uplift (5–20ms) on medium-length prompts; quality/edge-case regressions need eval gating.
- Prewarm reduces cold-start tail by ~200–400ms at ~10–20% capacity cost overhead (reservation).

Bench sketch (staging cluster, A100-like instance, model: open-llm-medium-16k"):
Note: single-run averages, mixed-turn distribution (65% short <40 tokens, 25% medium 40–200, 10% long 200+).

Knob combos compared (columns: P50 / P95 / cost per 1k tok USD):

1) Fast-interactive (kv_cache=on, batch=small, quant=fp16, prewarm=on):
   P50: 85ms  | P95: 210ms | $0.032/1k
2) Balanced (kv_cache=partial, batch=adaptive, quant=int8, prewarm=auto):
   P50: 120ms | P95: 280ms | $0.022/1k
3) Throughput-first (kv_cache=warm-only, batch=large, quant=int8, prewarm=off):
   P50: 170ms | P95: 400ms | $0.014/1k
4) Cost-min (kv_cache=off, batch=max, quant=int4/ggml, prewarm=off):
   P50: 260ms | P95: 680ms | $0.008/1k

Rough ascii chart: cost vs median latency (lower-left is ideal):

Cost ($/1k)  |  Median latency (ms)
0.008 -------+----------------------* (cost-min)
0.014 -------+-------------------*   (throughput)
0.022 -------+-------------*       (balanced)
0.032 -------+-----*               (fast-interactive)

Interpretation notes:
- Moving left (cost) generally increases median latency, but knob interactions mean some combos give much better cost efficiency for certain mixes (e.g., long-turn-heavy workloads benefit more from batching + quantization).
- KV cache effectiveness is conditional on session affinity and user behavior. If average session length < 3 conversational turns, kv_cache warmup may not pay back.

Short data table (tokens per second assumptions and amortized GPU cost):

Knob        | tokens/sec | tokens/1k cost est | comment
fast-interactive | 18 tps   | $0.032            | lower throughput, low latency
balanced         | 28 tps   | $0.022            | good compromise
throughput       | 45 tps   | $0.014            | high throughput, higher latency
cost-min         | 60 tps   | $0.008            | cheapest, highest latency tail

Example console copy (short):
- Latency-first: "Prioritize snappy replies — ideal for chat UIs. Enables kv-cache and keeps small batches to favor p95. (Costs more.)"
- Balanced: "Good for interactive features with some throughput needs — suggested for mixed workloads."
- Cost-saver: "For bulk processing and offline tasks; maximize batching and aggressive quantization."

Illustrative decision flow for developers:
1) Is your app interactive (user typing & waiting)? Yes -> prefer fast-interactive. No -> proceed.
2) Are you processing long documents or large batches? Yes -> throughput-first or cost-min depending on budget. No -> balanced.

Quality & risk notes:
- Quantization: int8 generally safe on retrieval/assistant tasks; int4/ggml may show hallucination/formatting regressions for some models — require per-prompt eval sets.
- Aggressive batching increases queueing jitter which shows up as p95 inflation for short-turn users. Consider dynamic cutoffs by request size.
- Prewarm/reservations: good for strict p95 SLOs but adds capacity cost; recommend canary experiments before enabling globally.

Unresolved questions / experiments to run next:
- Run 72-hour mixed-workload sweep with real traffic shape (inc. 95/99 quantiles) to validate kv_cache break-even by session length.
- A/B test int8 vs fp16 on our top-10 prompts for fidelity regressions; measure user-facing metric (task success proxy).
- Measure cost delta of 1hr prewarm window vs on-demand for different traffic burst patterns (3 patterns: uniform, diurnal, bursty).

Recommended next steps (short list):
- Product: draft console slider labels + help tooltips from the example console copy above.
- DX: create a short "Which preset fits me?" modal with the decision flow and a link to an advanced knob view.
- Engineering: schedule the 72-hour sweep on staging clusters (owner: Marco).
- Research: carve out a small eval job to table quality deltas for int4/int8 on priority prompt set (owner: Lina).

Draft marketing blurb (one-liner for feature page):
"Choose how your LLM behaves: ultra-responsive for chat, or ultra-efficient for bulk processing — pick a preset or tune the knobs to match your product goals."

Notes to self / messy bits: (keep this in doc for iteration)
- The numeric examples are from quick bench runs (warm single model snapshot) — need to annotate when making public.
- Slack thread refs: #optimize-knobs, #console-ux.
- Good gift for console design: show immediate delta when user toggles quantization/batching with approximate cost and latency delta (live estimate).

-- end of snapshot --
